title: Dynamic Spectrum of Thyroid Diseases: From Mechanistic Understanding to Management Approaches
authors: Parul Gupta, Alka Singh, Prof. S.K. Verma
affiliations: \Affiliated to V. B. S. Purvanchal University, Jaunpur, Uttar Pradesh, India 222002

blocks.x: Abstract:

The heterogeneity of thyroid diseases among populations with different nutrition, environmental toxicants, and lifestyle around the world suggests that thyroid diseases are multifactorial endocrine diseases characterized by complex networking of multiple molecular and physiological actions. They include autoimmunological disruption, hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid (HPT)-axis dysregulation, micronutrient-dependent enzymatic action on hormone biosynthesis, and constitutive genomic susceptibility. These are combined with varying population levels of iodine and selenium intake, exposure to endocrine-disrupting chemicals, and population-level variation in lifestyle and diet across geographical areas. This chapter considers the mechanistic hypotheses and epidemiologic evidence available on major thyroid diseases, and describes the dynamics of hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, autoimmune thyroid diseases, and iodine-induced thyroid dysfunction across diverse populations. The role of the interaction between environmental exposures, population patterns of nutrition, and genetic or biological susceptibility in determining the global burden, the phenotypic spectrum, and the clinical complexity of thyroid diseases is stressed. It also integrates these insights into mechanisms-based management models for precision diagnostics, micronutrient modulation, stratified risk profiling, and context- and mechanism-based therapeutic interventions.
Keywords: Autoimmune thyroid disease; Environmental exposures; Graves’ disease; Hyperthyroidism; Hypothyroidism; Iodine deficiency.
1. Introduction:

Approximately 42 million people in India are affected by thyroid disorders. Globally, approximately 200 million people live with some form of thyroid disorder. Two major thyroid conditions are hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, with hypothyroidism being more common. Thyroid gland acts as a master controller of metabolism, growth, and development, and its activity is regulated by the hypothalamus-pituitary-thyroid axis. Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) secreted by the hypothalamus causes the release of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) from the anterior pituitary gland, which further regulates thyroid hormone synthesis. It produces thyroxine (T4) in higher quantities (~93%), with a minor amount of triiodothyronine (T3) (~7%). T3 has greater biological activity than T4, and its synthesis occurs via the peripheral conversion of T4 (Mansoor et al., 2011). Thyroid hormones play a bidirectional role in homeostasis, functioning as metabolic regulators

They influence a wide range of metabolic activities and are regulated mainly by pituitary thyrotropin (TSH), which is widely used as a diagnostic indicator of thyroid dysfunction (Hoermann et al., 2015). Understanding the dynamic relationship between the underlying mechanisms and clinical manifestations is important for better disease management (Chakera et al., 2012). Treating these conditions can be complicated in many cases because thyroid hormone levels tend to fluctuate, sometimes unpredictably because of vague symptoms and signs such as fatigue, fluctuations in weight, palpitations and may take several weeks to adjust.
2. Dynamic Spectrum of Thyroid Disorders:
2.1. Hypothyroidism:

Primary hypothyroidism arises from thyroid gland dysfunction, leading to inadequate production of thyroid hormones to meet the body's metabolic demand. It is the most common endocrine disorder with a prevalence of about 3.8%-4.6%. Autoimmune thyroiditis is the predominant cause of primary hypothyroidism in the Western population whereas iodine deficiency remains prevent worldwide. Additional causes of hypothyroidism include thyroidectomy, radioiodine therapy and various medications such as amiodarone, lithium, iodine, interferon, thionamide, thalidomide, and rifampicin (Chakera et al., 2012). Hypothyroidism can cause many mild and nonspecific clinical manifestations, including weight gain, fatigue, poor concentration, menstrual irregularities, cold intolerance, constipation, and dry skin (Gutch et al., 2013). Overt hypothyroidism is biochemically defined by an elevated serum thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration along with decreased free T4 concentration. In contrast, subclinical hypothyroidism is defined as an increased TSH concentration with normal free T4 levels. The typical population reference range for TSH is approximately 0.4-4.5 mIU/L and TSH values above 10 mIU/L are typically observed in overt hypothyroidism (Chakera et al., 2012). During pregnancy, thyroid function evaluation should be based on trimester-specific reference ranges for TSH. When such ranges are unavailable, then the upper reference limits are taken as 2.5 mIU/L in the first trimester and 3 mIU/L in the second and third trimester (Abalovich et al., 2007) (Stagnaro-Green et al., 2011).
2.2. Hyperthyroidism:

Hyperthyroidism is a clinical condition defined as a hypermetabolic state by elevated concentrations of free thyroxine (T4) and free triiodothyronine (T3) in the bloodstream (LiVolsi and Baloch, 2018). The prevalence of hyperthyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions worldwide is estimated to range from approximately 0.2-2.5% (Taylor et al., 2018). Overt hypothyroidism characterized by suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels with elevated triiodothyronine (T3) and/or free thyroxine (T4). In contrast, subclinical hyperthyroidism is defined as suppressed TSH levels with normal circulating free T4 and T3 levels (Chung, 2020) (Lee and Pearce, 2023). The prevalence of hyperthyroidism in the United States is approximately 1.2% including 0.5% overt hyperthyroidism and 0.7% subclinical hyperthyroidism. The condition is predominantly caused by Graves’ disease (GD), toxic multinodular goiter (TMNG), and toxic adenoma (TA) (Singer et al., 1995). Hyperthyroidism influences cardiovascular function through increased heart rate, contractility, systolic hypertension, altered peripheral vascular resistance, atrial fibrillation and hypercoagulability (Sohn et al., 2020). Graves’ disease is the leading cause of hyperthyroidism in the iodine-sufficient region, with a prevalence of approximately 2% in women and 0.5% in men (Ippolito et al., 2021). The clinical manifestations of hyperthyroidism include weight loss with normal or increased appetite, palpitations, anxiety, excessive sweating, insomnia and heat intolerance (Prisant et al., 2006).
2.3. Autoimmune Thyroid Diseases:

Autoimmune thyroid diseases (AITD) such as Graves’ disease (GD) and Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (HT) are widely recognized as major contributors to public health burden. Affecting nearly 1-5% of population, they represent both the most prevalent thyroid disorders and the most frequent autoimmune diseases (Tomer 2014). The defining clinical hallmarks of Graves’ disease and Hashimoto's thyroiditis are thyrotoxicosis and hypothyroidism respectively. Autoimmune thyroid diseases (AITD) affect 5% of the population. Approximately 20% of AITD risk is attributed to environmental influences such as radiation, iodine levels, infection, stress, smoking and drugs (Antonelli et al., 2015). In Graves' disease, lymphocytic infiltration promotes the activation of TSH receptor (TSHR)-reactive B cells, leading to the production of TSHR-stimulating antibodies, resulting in hyperthyroidism. In contrast, Hashimoto's thyroiditis involves apoptotic destruction of thyroid cells, leading to hypothyroidism (Hasham and Tomer, 2012).
3. Biological Mechanisms Underlying Thyroid Disorders:
3.1. Hypothalamus-Pituitary-Thyroid (HPT) Axis:

Thyroid hormones act as a systematic master regulator, which is not only essential for neonatal development and maturation but also for maintaining metabolic equilibrium throughout adulthood (Gavrila & Hollenberg, 2019). Thyroid hormone production is regulated by hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid (HPT) axis, a neuroendocrine loop in which circulating thyroid hormone levels mediate negative feedback on both the hypothalamus and pituitary gland. Hypothalamic neurons secrete thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), stimulating the release of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) from the anterior pituitary. TSH binds to receptors on follicular thyrocytes, which produce two thyroid hormones, thyroxine (T4), and triiodothyronine (T3) from thyroglobulin (Keestra et al., 2020). In healthy individuals, approximately 20% of daily T3 (the active hormone) is directly produced by the thyroid gland, whereas the remaining 80% is generated peripherally via iodothyronine deiodinases (Maia et al., 2005). After secretion, thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) circulate in the bloodstream bound to proteins such as thyroid hormone-binding globulin, transthyretin, and albumin. More than 99% of circulating thyroid hormones remain bound, with only 1% available in the free form for tissue uptake (Yen et al., 2006).

3.2. Genetic and Epigenetic Susceptibility:

Graves' disease is acquired by individuals who have an inherent genetic predisposition and are subjected to environmental triggers that interfere with the body’s ability to accept its tissues in the central and peripheral levels (Stefan et al., 2014). There are various environmental triggers that are known to increase the risk of AITD, such as an iodine imbalance (both excessive and insufficient amounts) and drugs like interferon-alpha (IFNα) and amiodarone, bacterial and viral infection (e.g. Yersinia Enterocolitica and hepatitis C virus), smoking, stress, and pollutants (e.g. polyaromatic hydrocarbons) (Cocks Eschler et al., 2011). Genetic susceptibility plays a dominant role in the etiology of AITD, with twin studies indicating that nearly 79% of disease susceptibility is attributable to genetic factors and showing higher concordance rates in monozygotic twins than in dizygotic twins (Jacobson et al., 2008). HLA-DR3 was the first gene found to be associated with both GD and HT. Since then, growing evidence has enhanced our understanding of genetic susceptibility and underlying mechanisms of thyroid autoimmunity. Numerous loci have now been implicated in AITD, including HLA-DR subtypes and two groups of non-MHC genes: immune-regulatory genes (CD40, CTLA-4, PTPN22, FOXP3, and CD25); and thyroid-specific genes (Thyroglobulin (Tg) and TSHR) (Hasham and Tomer, 2012).

Epigenetics is the study of non-genetic mechanisms on gene expression leading to phenotypes. These consist of DNA methylation, histone modification, and non-coding RNA interference. When epigenetics affects the genes involved in the immune system and thyroid system, there will be a dysfunction resulting in autoimmune diseases (Wang et al., 2017).
4. Environmental and Nutritional Factors:

Environmental and nutritional elements are major determinants in the pathogenesis of thyroid disorders. Among those individuals genetically predisposed to AITD, environmental factors can play a critical role in the development of autoimmune thyroid disease (AITD). They may involve excessive intake of iodine, deficiency of selenium and vitamin D, as well as exposure to radiation due to either nuclear fallout or specific types of therapy (Ferrari et al., 2017). Autoimmune thyroiditis is another term for AITD that results from the combination of genetic, environmental, and nutritional aspects. Concerning nutrition, minerals such as iodine, iron, and selenium determine thyroid physiology (Rayman 2019).
4.1. Iodine Intake:

Besides being a crucial component of thyroid hormones, iodine plays an important role in maintaining a healthy thyroid cell environment to promote their growth and function (Sun et al., 2014). Over the past few decades, the global iodine supplementation programs, especially universal salt iodization, have significantly reduced iodine deficiency. However, excessive iodine intake is now more common and can trigger autoimmune thyroid disease. Iodine deficiency arising from insufficient dietary intake is particularly observed in remote inland areas lacking access to marine foods and is a major cause of developmental delays, intellectual disability, endemic goiter and other health complications (Luo et al., 2014). Differences in iodine intake among the population significantly influence the global prevalence of thyroid dysfunction. Nodular thyroid disorders are more common in iodine-deficient regions, whereas autoimmune thyroid diseases, including Hashimoto's thyroiditis and Graves' disease are more frequently observed in iodine-sufficient population (Taylor et al., 2018).
4.2. Role of Micronutrients:

Several nutritional factors, apart from iodine, have been shown to influence thyroid function. Goitrogens are naturally occurring dietary compounds that interfere with thyroid function and lead to gland enlargement. They are mainly found in cruciferous vegetables and soy products (Babiker et al., 2020). Cruciferous vegetables belong to the Brassicaceae family such as kale, turnips, cauliflower and other related vegetables (Babiker et al., 2020). Cruciferous vegetables are rich in thioglycosides which are metabolized into thiocyanates which can inhibit iodine uptake and its incorporation into thyroglobulin, resulting in increased TSH secretion and enhanced thyroid cells proliferation (Truong et al., 2010). Selenium is present in high concentration in the thyroid gland (0.2-2 μg/g), representing the highest selenium content per gram among all organs due to its richness in selenoproteins. Incorporated into these proteins, selenium exerts potent antioxidant activity, helping to defend thyroid tissue by eliminating reactive oxygen species produced during the synthesis of thyroid hormones (Ventura et al., 2017).
4.3. Lifestyle Related Factors:

Lifestyle related factors play a crucial role in the development of thyroid disorders, including smoking, unhealthy dietary habits, alcohol consumption, poor sleep patterns, physical inactivity, and obesity. Smoking is strongly associated with the development of Graves' hyperthyroidism (GH), especially Graves' ophthalmology (GO) (Huang et al., 2019).

Alcohol is the third largest risk factor leading cause of disease and disability globally, directly causing over 60 types of diseases and contributing to nearly 200 others (World Health Organization, 2011). It exerts multiple efforts on the hypothalamus-pituitary-thyroid axis and thyroid gland function, including direct suppression via cellular toxicity and indirect inhibition by blunting the response of thyrotropin-releasing hormone (Balhara and Deb, 2013).
5. Mechanism based management strategies:
Mechanism based management focuses on targeting the pathophysiological mechanisms rather than only controlling symptoms.

Levothyroxine (LT4) has long been the standard treatment of hypothyroidism. It is effective when administered orally, exhibits a long serum half-life that supports convenient daily doses, and leads to the improvement or resolution of the symptoms in the majority of patients (Jonklaas et al., 2014). Thionamides are the main antithyroid drugs, which are preferred as first-choice for the treatment of Graves' disease, including propylthiouracil (PTU), methimazole (MMI) and carbimazole (CBZ). PTU and MMI are rapidly and almost completely absorbed following oral administration, reaching peak serum concentrations within 1-2 hours in a dose dependent manner. Antithyroid drugs serve a dual role in the treatment of hyperthyroidism, functioning as long term therapy (1-2 years) and as a short term use to prepare patients for radiometabolic or surgical procedures (Fumarola et al., 2010).

Potassium perchlorate is utilized in the treatment of thyrotoxicosis associated with excess iodine exposure, particularly in type 1 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis. The drugs inhibit iodide transport into thyroid cells and promote its release (Fumarola et al., 2010).

Sodium ipoiodate and iopanoic acid which are iodinated contrast media, reduce the peripheral conversion of T4 into T3 by approximately 70% and are used in thyrotoxicosis crisis, pre-operative preparation and as an alternative therapy in patients with hypersensitivity to antithyroid drugs (Fumarola et al., 2010).
6. Conclusion:

Thyroid-related diseases are not fixed but dynamic, influenced by both genetic and environmental factors. An evaluation of their mechanisms makes it easy to understand the onset, progression and clinical manifestations of these conditions. A better understanding of these mechanisms has allowed the generation of treatment strategies based on such mechanisms. Incorporating our knowledge with an approach that focuses on the patient’s well-being is vital for the early detection of diseases, effective treatment, and successful outcomes of disease. Moving forward, attention needs to shift towards precision medicine and prevention to address the wider spectrum of thyroid disorders.
